The corresponding sheet music rendered from this ABC sequence is shown in Fig. 4. In this example, the structure of ABC
notation starts with a header that includes:

• X (Tune Number): This is a unique number assigned to the tune, serving as a reference in collections or databases.

• L (Unit Note Length): This defines the default duration of notes. In this context, 1/8 indicates that each note is an
eighth note, which is a standard choice for folk tunes.

• M (Meter): This denotes the time signature of the piece, which determines the rhythmic pulse. Here, 3/4 suggests a
waltz-like rhythm.

• K (Key): This sets the key signature for the tune. D signifies that the piece is in the key of D major.

After the header, the body of the ABC notation consists of the musical notes themselves. Each note is represented by a letter
(A to G), which corresponds to the pitch. The octaves are indicated by lower-cased letters or apostrophes for higher octaves
and upper-cased letters or commas for lower or higher octaves, respectively. The duration of notes is modified by numbers;

A.2. MIDI

MIDI, short for Musical Instrument Digital Interface, is a technical standard that describes a protocol, digital interface, and
connectors and allows a wide variety of electronic musical instruments, computers, and other related devices to connect and
communicate with one another. Unlike ABC notation, which is designed for human readability and the transcription of
musical scores, MIDI is focused on capturing and conveying information about music performance and production in a
format that machines can interpret and process.

The core of MIDI communication involves MIDI messages, which are digital signals that represent various musical elements
such as notes, pitch, velocity (how hard a note is played), control changes (modifications to sound parameters), and program
changes (instrument changes). These messages do not transmit audio; instead, they send instructions about how music
should be played or produced. This approach allows MIDI to be incredibly versatile and lightweight compared to raw audio,
suitable for real-time control during live performances and detailed editing in studio environments.

MIDI files, commonly with the extension .mid or .midi, store sequences of MIDI messages that can be played back by
computer software or electronic instruments. These files make it possible to share and distribute musical compositions in a
form that can be easily modified, transposed, or played back with different instrument sounds, offering a level of flexibility
and creative freedom that is unique to the digital music domain.

2https://abcnotation.com/wiki/abc:standard:v2.1

15 Beyond Language Models: Byte Models are Digital World Simulators

There are several ways to create and edit MIDI, each catering to different workflows and preferences:

• MIDI Keyboards and Controllers : Physical devices that allow musicians to input notes and control data into a
computer. They emulate traditional instruments and can capture the nuances of a performance in MIDI format.

• Piano Roll: A graphical interface in digital audio workstations (as shown in Fig. 1) where notes are displayed and
edited on a grid representing pitch and time. It is intuitive for composing melodies, chords, and rhythms.

• Score Editor: Allows users to input and edit music in traditional notation, converting written notes into MIDI data.
Ideal for those familiar with musical notation.

• Programming and Scripting: Involves writing code to generate and manipulate MIDI data, offering complex and
generative musical possibilities beyond manual input methods. For instance, complex MIDI sequences and automation
can be generated using software such as Max/MSP, Pure Data, or programming languages (e.g., SuperCollider).

Although MIDI offers immense benefits for musicians and producers, when converting MIDI data back into score-oriented
symbolic music formats like ABC notation, certain challenges arise due to the intrinsic differences between these formats.
MIDI excels at capturing how a piece of music is played, including the timing, velocity, and expressiveness of each note. In
contrast, ABC notation focuses on the structural elements of music, such as melody, harmony, and rhythm, using a textual
format that is more accessible for human reading and writing but less detailed in terms of performance nuances.

subsequently back to ABC notation. The corresponding sheet music, rendered from this ABC sequence, is shown in Fig.
5. One can observe that the ABC sequence and the musical score appear significantly longer than the original due to
the elimination of repeat signs in MIDI, requiring repeated sections to be explicitly written out. Additionally, the bar
divisions and the ornaments in the MIDI-to-ABC conversion might not align perfectly with the original ABC notation.
These ornaments are often represented as a series of rapid notes in MIDI, which can complicate their translation back into
ABC notation.

While MIDI-rendered sheet music and its ABC notation counterpart may sound identical when performed, the visual
complexity of the MIDI transcription can make it more challenging to read than the ABC version. This discrepancy
underscores the fact that MIDI and ABC are formats tailored for different contexts. MIDI is adept at capturing nuanced
performance data, such as dynamics and subtle timing variations, which are essential for playback fidelity but are not as
visually straightforward as ABC notation. On the other hand, ABC notation, with its simplified symbolic representation, is
not ideal for conveying detailed performance information.

Both formats have overlapping capabilities in representing musical information, yet each also possesses unique characteristics
that do not translate perfectly when converting from one to the other. This results in a loss of information: nuances specific
to each format can be diminished or omitted entirely during the conversion process. Such losses present a challenge in
preserving the full intent and detail of a musical piece when moving between ABC and MIDI formats.

B. CPU States Dataset

The CPU States Dataset has been crafted using a Python script to simulate the operations of a CPU, offering a controlled
environment to assess the capabilities of bGPT in modelling the hardware behaviour. This appendix offers an overview of
the dataset, introducing the structure, instruction set, and details of the dataset curation.

16 Beyond Language Models: Byte Models are Digital World Simulators

The dataset comprises entries of 1KB memory blocks, each paired with a subsequent 16-byte sequence representing the
CPU register states. The memory blocks encode varying numbers of machine instructions, while the register state sequence
includes the CPU status post-execution of each instruction. The CPU registers in each state consist of:

• Program Counter (PC): 1 byte in size, points to the next instruction in the memory.

• Accumulator (ACC): A 1-byte register involved in arithmetic and logic operations.

• Instruction Register (IR): Occupies 4 bytes, storing the currently executed instruction.

• General-Purpose Registers: An additional 10 bytes are allocated, emulating a range of registers (labelled A-J) used
for various computational purposes.

Transitions between states mimic the execution cycle of a CPU, including fetching instructions from memory, decoding
them to determine the required operation, and executing the operation to modify the state. The execution process includes
instructions for modifying register values, performing arithmetic calculations, and controlling the program flow.

Each instruction in the dataset is encoded in a four-byte format OP ADDR1 ADDR2 ADDR3 , with each byte serving a
specific purpose:

• OP (Operation Code): 1 byte representing the opcode of the instruction to be executed.

• ADDR1, ADDR2, ADDR3: 1 byte each, representing up to three addresses that the instruction may interact with.

The opcode and addresses together describe the action to be taken by the CPU. The instructions vary in terms of the number
of addresses they use, from zero-address to three-address instructions. This variability allows the simulation of a wide range
of operations, from simple data movement to complex arithmetic and logical functions.

Table 7 (located on page 19) details the instruction set and the variants each instruction can have, depending on the values in
the address fields. The variant to be executed is determined by the non-zero value in the address fields. For zero-address
instructions, all address fields are zero. For single-address instructions, ADDR1 holds the address of the register involved,
and the other fields are zero. For two- and three-address instructions, the respective fields hold the addresses of the registers
involved in the operation.

In designing the instruction set, complex instructions like jump commands were deliberately excluded to prevent the
occurrence of infinite loops or other complexities that could hinder straightforward simulation.

The Python script generates the CPU States Dataset by randomly initializing the ACC and general-purpose registers for each
simulation, thereby ensuring a wide range of starting conditions. It then executes a random sequence of instructions, varying
in length from 1 to 256, with the effect of each instruction on the CPU state being recorded. This results in a sequence of
states that reflects the cumulative impact of the executed instructions. The script guarantees that each sequence culminates
with a halt instruction HLT, marking the end of a program. Furthermore, when considering only the register changes related
to instructions, there are over 516 million potential scenarios resulting from combinations of various instruction types,
registers, and their values.

The dataset thus produced comprises 2.1 million entries for the training set and 21,000 entries for the evaluation set. This
process, with its random initial states and varied instruction lengths, produces a diverse dataset that is essential for training
and evaluating the effectiveness of bGPT in modelling CPU states.

expectations: identify the paper's method before applying method-specific criteria

synthesis.contribution_summary: The paper introduces bGPT, a hierarchical Transformer trained by next-byte prediction, as a unified model for binary data across media modalities and for native binary tasks. Beyond text, audio and image classification, it evaluates the model on ABC↔MIDI symbolic music conversion and on CPU state prediction, which the authors frame as algorithm and hardware simulation. For the latter, the paper introduces a CPU States dataset of about 2.1 million instances. It also reports scaling experiments, including a performance jump on the conversion task that the authors describe as emergent.
synthesis.originality: By the paper's own account, the method is not where the originality lies. The Background section credits ByteFormer and MegaByte with modelling raw byte sequences across modalities, and states that bGPT adapts a hierarchical Transformer architecture from prior work that includes MegaByte. The inspected text does not state an architectural difference from MegaByte. The more distinctive element is the task framing: it treats format conversion and CPU state transitions as byte-sequence modelling, introduces a CPU States dataset, and positions ABC↔MIDI conversion as a new task because prior music models avoided modelling MIDI directly. These comparisons reflect the authors' descriptions of the cited works and were not independently verified. The 'paradigm shift' framing claims more than the related-work section concedes. A clear statement of what differs from MegaByte, and a comparison against MegaByte or ByteFormer on the native-binary tasks, would show whether any methodological novelty exists beyond the task and dataset contributions.
synthesis.likely_impact: The work could interest researchers on neural emulators, binary analysis and reverse-engineering, learned format converters, and token-free foundation models. A released CPU-state task and dataset could seed a benchmark line for byte models as simulators of digital processes. Several factors may limit its influence. The evaluation uses a simplified synthetic CPU that excludes jump instructions. CPU accuracy is measured byte-wise, with no trivial baselines. Conversion is reported only as BPB, without exact-match rates. Media results trail modality-specific baselines, and no other byte model is compared. Influence will likely come more from the framing and dataset than from bGPT as a model.
synthesis.decision_synthesis:
The strongest case for the paper is its reframing of byte models as simulators of algorithms and hardware. The concrete CPU States dataset and the ABC↔MIDI task make that direction testable. The main concerns are about whether the evidence supports the claims.

(1) The abstract says bGPT 'matches specialized models'. Table 3, however, places the best bGPT variant below baselines on all three media tasks: by about 2 points on AG News and Speech Commands, and by about 9.4 points on CIFAR-10 (88.69% vs 98.13%). The baselines come from original studies with ImageNet pre-training. All results are single runs without variance, and no byte-model baseline is included.

(2) The 99.99% CPU accuracy is computed byte-wise on a jump-free synthetic CPU. Many state bytes may be trivially predictable, for example unchanged registers and an incrementing program counter. Without a copy-previous-state baseline, per-state or per-program exact match, and clarity on whether evaluation conditions on ground-truth prior states, this number may overstate simulation ability. Table 6 also suggests a threshold-like jump from 27% to near-perfect accuracy between 10^4 and 10^5 instances, followed by saturation; this is an advisory reading of three scale points.

(3) The ABC→MIDI result of 0.0011 BPB is a likelihood measure, not the 'error rate' the abstract calls it. The reverse direction is weaker (0.0789). The 'emergent ability' claim rests on a jump around epoch 11 in a single training run.

The score-changing questions for the authors are:
- How does bGPT differ from MegaByte, and how do MegaByte or ByteFormer perform on these tasks?
- What are the trivial baselines and exact-match rates for the CPU and conversion tasks?
- Is the epoch-11 jump reproducible across seeds?
- How will the generality claims be rescoped in light of Table 3?

Non-blocking improvements are to align the abstract wording with the tables and to state the architectural differences from prior hierarchical byte models explicitly.

claim_support.reasoning: The paper's own results show a roughly 9.4-point gap on images, which contradicts 'matches' for that modality. In addition, the vision and audio baseline numbers are copied from the original studies rather than run under shared settings. A gap of nearly 10 points on CIFAR-10, along with gaps on AG News and Speech Commands, contradicts 'matches'. This affects the media-modelling contribution.
points: The linked numeric claims match the tables, but the abstract's claim that bGPT 'matches specialized models' overstates Table 3, especially on CIFAR-10.
The abstract claims bGPT 'matches specialized models', but Table 3 shows clear gaps, most notably 88.69% vs 98.13% on CIFAR-10.

significance.reasoning: No grounded, candidate-targeted finding for this axis.

originality.reasoning: By the authors' own description, prior work already models multimodal byte sequences with hierarchical Transformers. The originality therefore rests on the task framing and the evaluation, not on the model itself. The difference from MegaByte and ByteFormer is author-reported and not verified here. The paper says the architecture is adapted from cited work. It also describes MegaByte (author-reported) as already modelling multi-modal byte sequences. The stated distinction therefore rests on native binary data and simulation tasks. The related-work section concedes only that prior work 'often neglects' native binary data, whereas the impact statement implies primacy. No technical difference from MegaByte is stated, and no comparison against it is reported.
points: The authors explicitly build bGPT's architecture on prior hierarchical byte models (MegaByte and others). The architectural novelty is therefore modest, and the claimed difference lies in applying the model to native binary data and simulation.

The paper explicitly adapts its architecture from prior hierarchical/patch byte models. Its originality therefore lies in the binary-native simulation framing and tasks, not the model design, yet the impact statement frames bGPT more broadly.

significance.reasoning: The paper studies byte-level modelling of native binary processes, a direction the authors describe as underexplored. A released task and dataset of this kind could enable follow-up work. The authors position the work against byte models that, as they describe them, address media or narrow tasks; evaluating byte models on algorithm/hardware simulation is a less-explored direction that could open a research agenda.
points: Applying a single next-byte-prediction model to both media files and native binary tasks (format conversion, CPU state simulation) is an interesting and potentially impactful framing.
Unified byte-level modelling extended to native binary tasks (algorithm and CPU simulation) is a distinctive, potentially impactful framing.

originality.reasoning: The paper reports two relevant facts. First, ByteFormer and MegaByte already model byte sequences across modalities. Second, bGPT adapts a hierarchical architecture from cited work that includes MegaByte. By the authors' own account, therefore, neither the model nor multimodal byte modelling is new. The 'paradigm shift' framing claims more than the related-work section concedes. The cited works are described here only as the authors report them; I have not verified them. The authors explicitly build on next-token prediction. Their stated distinction is native binary data combined with broad evaluation. The originality claimed is therefore one of scope and evaluation, which is coherent with the related-work section.
points: The authors present bGPT as a new byte model and a general digital world simulator. Their own Background section says byte-level modelling across modalities already exists, and that the architecture is adapted from prior work. Originality therefore lies mainly in the application framing and the native-binary tasks, not in the model.
The authors claim to introduce bGPT for binary data and digital world modelling. They build on next-token prediction and position against media-focused byte models.

Against that positioning, treating format conversion and CPU state transitions as sequence modelling is a distinct and testable research direction. claim_support.reasoning: Accuracy is computed per byte rather than per state or per program. Many register bytes are unchanged between steps, so a copy-previous-state baseline could already score high, and the paper reports no such baseline. In addition, with no jumps, the program counter increments trivially. First, byte-wise accuracy over full register states may be dominated by bytes that a single instruction leaves unchanged. That could make the metric look stronger than the correctness of the actual state updates. Second, the authors acknowledge that the CPU is simplified, which limits generalization to 'simulating CPU behaviour'. Many state bytes, such as the PC and unchanged registers, are trivially predictable. Byte-wise accuracy therefore inflates the measure of execution fidelity. The task also excludes control flow.
points: The CPU 99.99% accuracy is measured byte-wise on a simplified, jump-free synthetic CPU with no simple baseline. This weakens the 'exceptional capabilities' and emergence claims.

The 99.99% CPU-state accuracy (C2) is a byte-wise metric on a CPU that the authors themselves describe as simplified. The inspected results do not report trace-level correctness, and there is no baseline.
The 99.99% CPU-state accuracy is computed byte-wise over a simplified CPU that has no jumps. Byte-wise accuracy can be high even when many full states are wrong.

claim_support.reasoning: Low BPB does not by itself establish that generated MIDI files are byte-exact or valid. A jump within one training run reflects optimization dynamics, not scale-driven emergence. A within-run loss drop (grokking-like) is not the scale-emergence of Wei et al.; with three data scales, one run each, the evidence is thin. Data-conversion 'emergence' claimed in summary is unsupported by any discontinuity shown. A single training-time jump at fixed model size is a training dynamic, not scale-induced emergence. The argument is also internally inconsistent: BPB is described as smooth while the claimed jump is visible in loss. The paper reports only one seed for this run. The jump occurs within a single training run rather than across scales. In addition, bGPT6's BPB equals bGPT5's (0.0969). Together these weaken the scaling and emergence framing.
points: The 0.0011 BPB result for ABC→MIDI is reported as conditional BPB. No exact-conversion success rate is given, and the 'emergent ability' claim rests on a training curve from a single run.
'Emergent abilities' rests on a single loss-curve jump at epoch 11, conflating training dynamics with scale emergence.
The 'emergent abilities' claim rests on a loss-curve jump for one run, and the paper's own rebuttal argument is weak.
The claims of 'strong scalability' and 'emergent abilities' rest on a few data scales and on a within-run loss jump. This is limited support for emergence.
